On the Doric form of the first syllable we have spoken under γάπεδον [ground].
neither plow nor earth-cutting mattock cuts the field.

That the use of this particle is to express either emphasis or diminution has been observed by Apollonius in Bekker's Anecdota p. 517, 24 and the scholiast on Dionysius Thrax ibid. p. 838, 10. 971, 13. Similarly Eustathius p. 969 end, although he errs in believing that among the poets it is sometimes expletive and used to avoid hiatus (πρὸς βύσιν χασμωδίας [for the avoidance of a gaping of sound]), which was also the opinion of Demetrius Triclinius and other grammarians of the lowest age, who corrupted not a few verses of the scenic poets where they wanted either to lengthen a short syllable or to correct a hiatus which the reading of the older books presented: which errors are sometimes combined with ignorance of prosody, of which sort is that they not rarely added γε to the particles ἄγαν [too much] and λίαν [excessively], since they considered the second syllable short. There is no Latin particle which exactly corresponds to the Greek one: yet often it can be suitably rendered by the Latin words certe, quidem, saltem, quippe. It is placed so that it is attached to the word in which the force of the sentence is perceived, except that when added to an article and a substantive or adjective it is generally placed between the article and the noun. Wellauer arranged the Aeschylean examples according to the kinds of words: which we present here with corrections throughout. Among these there are some in which it is not attached to the word to which it especially belongs, but is transposed on account of metrical necessity without any loss of meaning, since it affects not only the word to which it is attached but the whole sentence.
where I have restored τοῦτο κοὐκ [this and not].
For thus rightly Porson for δέ [but].
